lines.text: Chapter 1: What the Fed is
lines.say: Chapter one. What the Fed actually is.

lines.text: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank.
lines.say: The Federal Reserve is America's central bank.

lines.text: It's the bank for banks and for the government, not for you and me.
lines.say: It's the bank for banks, and for the government. It's not a bank for you and me.

lines.text: Congress created it with the Federal Reserve Act, signed on December 23, 1913.
lines.say: Congress created it with the Federal Reserve Act, which President Woodrow Wilson signed on December twenty-third, nineteen thirteen.

lines.text: Before that, bank panics kept wiping out savers, and there was no lender of last resort.
lines.say: Before that, bank panics kept wiping people out, and there was nobody to lend to banks in an emergency.

lines.text: The Fed isn't one building. It's 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, plus a Board in Washington.
lines.say: The Fed isn't one building. It's twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, plus a Board of Governors in Washington.

lines.text: The regional banks also supervise banks, run payment systems, and handle the government's accounts.

lines.text: The Board has 7 governors, each appointed for a 14-year term.

lines.text: Chapter 2: The job
lines.say: Chapter two. The job.

lines.text: Congress gave the Fed its job in 1977: maximum employment and stable prices.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy-seven, Congress spelled out the Fed's job: maximum employment and stable prices.

lines.text: People call it the dual mandate. The law also mentions moderate long-term interest rates.

lines.text: Stable prices doesn't mean zero inflation. Since 2012, the Fed's goal has been 2% a year.

lines.text: Why not zero? A little inflation gives the Fed room to cut rates when things go wrong.

lines.text: And outright falling prices can make people wait to buy, which can slow the whole economy.

lines.text: Chapter 3: The main lever
lines.say: Chapter three. The main lever.

lines.text: The Fed's headline tool is the federal funds rate.
lines.say: The Fed's headline tool is something called the federal funds rate.

lines.text: It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.

lines.text: The Fed doesn't set one number. It sets a target range, like 3.75% to 4%.

lines.text: Then it steers the market into that range with a few tools.
lines.say: Then it steers the market into that range with a few tools.

lines.text: The big one: the Fed pays banks interest on money they park at the Fed.
lines.say: The big one is that the Fed pays banks interest on money they park at the Fed.

lines.text: No bank wants to lend to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to sit still.
lines.say: No bank wants to lend to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to just sit still.

lines.text: Banks can also borrow straight from the Fed at the discount window, usually at a higher rate. It's the emergency backstop.

lines.text: So how does a rate between banks reach your wallet? Through a chain.

lines.text: Credit cards feel it fastest. Most card rates follow the prime rate.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Fighting inflation

lines.text: Why would raising rates lower prices? Because it makes borrowing and spending more expensive.

post.title: The Federal Reserve, explained from zero: who sets rates and how they hit your wallet
post.ig: 12 people decide what your loans cost. Here's how the Fed actually works.
post.tiktok: 12 people decide what your loans cost. The Fed, explained from zero.
post.yt_desc:
The Federal Reserve is America's central bank: 12 regional banks, a 7-member Board, and a 12-member committee that sets interest rates 8 times a year. On September 16, 2026 it raised its target range to 3.75%-4%, the first hike since 2023, with inflation at 3.4% in August 2026. We walk through the dual mandate, how the fed funds rate reaches credit cards, savings and mortgages, the math on a $400,000 mortgage at 3% vs 7%, the 1980 and 2022 inflation fights, and the Fed's $6.7 trillion balance sheet.
